endorsements.title: CHAI AI governance frameworks (playbooks)
endorsements.quote: HDOs should establish a structured, recurring training program that ensures all relevant staff (across clinical, administrative, technical, and leadership roles) understand the purpose, intended use, and known limitations of each AI system deployed within their environment.

endorsements.title: Top three priorities for artificial intelligence integration into emergency, critical, and perioperative medicine: an interdisciplinary clinical expert consensus
endorsements.issuer: Journal of anesthesia, analgesia and critical care
endorsements.quote: AI education should be tiered by role and aligned with digital competence levels, from foundational to expert

commentary.bottom_line: No supplied study tests role- and risk-tiered AI training, and no supplied study documents harm from uniform training, so this recommendation rests on two endorsements alone. A CHAI governance playbook and an interdisciplinary expert consensus both call for structured training, and the consensus specifically favors tiering by role and digital competence.

perspectives.view: The evidence base contains zero studies testing the practice and zero studies documenting the hazard. The support comes from one framework and one expert commentary, which GRADE treats as opinion rather than evidence. Certainty about whether tiered training changes user behavior or patient outcomes cannot be rated above no direct evidence.

The hazard holds that uniform training leaves users of high-risk, overreliance-prone tools under-prepared. No supplied study measures overreliance, error rates, or harm by training depth. Without such data, a health system cannot yet judge whether added training for high-risk tools catches errors before they reach patients, or how much benefit more frequent refreshers would add.

commentary.research_gap: Studies are needed that compare tiered and uniform training for the same AI tools and that measure user overreliance, detection of AI errors, and patient outcomes. They should also report the effects of different refresher intervals and the staff time each training tier requires.
commentary.underserved_note: No study tested the practice, so no evidence covers Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. Health systems serving these groups cannot tell from this evidence whether tiered training affects AI-related errors in their patients, and safety-net settings with thin staffing may face training burdens that no study has measured.
